message.content:
**Earliest historical reference (outside the New Testament)**  
The first non‑Christian source that mentions Jesus Christ is the Jewish historian **Flavius Josephus** in his *Antiquities of the Jews* (Book 18, Chapter 3). Josephus wrote this work around **93–94 CE** (the “Year 93” of the Jewish calendar, which corresponds to 93 CE). In the passage known as the *Testimonium Flavianum*, Josephus briefly describes Jesus as a wise man, a doer of “wonderful works,” and notes that he was crucified under Pontius Pilate.

> *“Now there was a wise man named Jesus, who was a doer of wonderful works. He was a teacher of people who were looking for truth. He attracted a large number of followers. He was crucified by Pilate, but the Christians who followed him did not give up their faith.”* (Antiquities 18.3.3)

This is the earliest surviving historical record that refers to Jesus by name and provides a brief account of his life and death.  

**Later early references**

| Source | Date | Key mention |
|--------|------|-------------|
| **Tacitus** – *Annals* 15.44 | 116 CE | “Christus, the founder of the name, was executed by Pontius Pilate.” |
| **Pliny the Younger** – *Letters* 10.96 | 112 CE | Mentions Christians worshipping Christ. |
| **Gospel of Mark** (Christian text) | ~70 CE | Earliest Christian narrative of Jesus. |

So, from a purely historical standpoint, **Josephus’s *Antiquities* (93–94 CE)** is the earliest reference to Jesus Christ.
